Between 50%-75% of the variance in IQ is genetic. End of story.

Note that this does not mean environmental factors cannot or have not driven IQ upwards. In fact, one of the reasons the genetic component of IQ may be so high today is that the environmental component of IQ is better controlled: IQ averages have gone up, while variance has gone down. That is to say, today the mean/sd are something like 100/15. In the past it would have been something like 70/30; which increases the variance (and decreases the heritability) by a factor of 4.

As we become better and better at optimizing the environment to maximize cognitive performance, the only remaining source for variability is genetics.

No. Flynn effect is a cultural IQ effect separate from in-cultural variance, and in-cultural variance shows 60-85% heritability. The APA likes to cite the lowest numbers they can come close to supporting because it makes them feel good, but 85%, within culture, is a lot closer than 60%.

The Flynn effect has caused average IQ gains that go beyond the percent of variance that can be attributed to environment in in-cultural studies. A person of an IQ of 50 or 60 is functionally VERY different in a higher-IQ society than one in a lower-IQ society. IQ is a proxy of intelligence and measures specific problem-solving and visualizing abilities. In cultures that don't nurture that kind of problem-solving, as a culture, a person with a low IQ isn't very functionally impaired. An Ashkenazi Jewish kid with an IQ of 50, though, is VERY unlikely to be able to live apart from a sheltered home and work environment. It means something completely different with them.
